Normalise f0 by speaker

Source: R/normalise.R
normalise_f0.Rd

Adds a within-speaker normalised f0 column to a long-format f0 data frame. Speaker normalisation puts contours from male and female speakers on a comparable scale, and is a near-universal pre-processing step before cross-speaker tone modelling, plotting, or contour summarisation (Rose 1987; Zhu 1999).

Three formulae are available. Semitones above or below the speaker's mean give a perceptually uniform scale. By-speaker z-scores combine centring with unit-variance scaling. Log z-scores (LZ) do both on a logarithmic scale: they are z-scores of log f0. Every formula relies on a per-speaker mean (and the z-scores on a per-speaker SD), which can be computed in two ways: over all observations alike, or so that every tone contributes equally whatever its number of tokens.

Usage

normalise_f0(
  data,
  f0 = "f0",
  speaker = "speaker",
  tone = "tone",
  method = c("semitone", "zscore", "lz"),
  mean_method = c("weighted", "simple"),
  sd_correction = TRUE
)

Arguments

data

A long-format data frame with one row per f0 sample. Must contain at least the f0, speaker, and (for "weighted" means) tone columns named below.

f0

Name of the column with raw f0 values, in Hz. Default "f0".

speaker

Name of the speaker ID column. Default "speaker".

tone

Name of the tone category column. Default "tone". Only read when mean_method = "weighted".

method

Normalisation formula. One of:

  • "semitone" (default): ST = 12 * log2(f0 / speaker_mean). Result is 0 at the speaker mean and ±12 at one octave above or below.

  • "zscore": Z = (f0 - speaker_mean) / s, where s is the speaker's SD of f0.

  • "lz": LZ = (log10(f0) - m) / s, where m and s are the speaker's mean and SD of log10 f0, as in Zhu (1999). Any base gives the same LZ, since it only rescales the logs.

With mean_method = "simple" both z-scores have mean 0 and SD 1 within each speaker (SD 1 as measured with the same sd_correction). With "weighted" the same holds with every tone counting equally: the per-tone means average to 0, while the plain mean over all observations moves away from 0 when tones have unequal numbers of observations.

mean_method

How the per-speaker mean, and the SD for the z-scores, are computed: "weighted" (default; every tone counts equally) or "simple" (all observations alike; the classic formula).

sd_correction

Logical: apply Bessel's correction to the SD. TRUE (default) uses the corrected (sample) SD, dividing by n - 1; FALSE the uncorrected (population) SD, dividing by n. Only affects "zscore" and "lz". See "The SD correction" below.

Value

The input data frame with two added columns:

  • speaker_mean: the per-speaker mean used for normalisation, in Hz. For "lz" this is the geometric mean, 10^m.

  • f0_st (if method = "semitone"), f0_zscore (if method = "zscore") or f0_lz (if method = "lz").

Details

What the function does internally

  1. Compute a per-speaker mean of f0 (of log f0 for "lz") using mean_method, and for the z-scores a per-speaker SD the same way (see below).

  2. Add that mean to data as a new column called speaker_mean.

  3. Apply the selected normalisation formula sample by sample and return the augmented data frame.

Choosing method

  • "semitone" is the standard for citation-tone work. The scale is perceptually uniform (one semitone is roughly one just-noticeable pitch step), centred on the speaker's own range, and preserves the logarithmic structure of musical pitch perception.

  • "zscore" is useful when both centring and scaling are desired, i.e., when you want to remove each speaker's baseline and equalise their f0 variability. Useful for cross-speaker statistical models where the raw variance differs strongly across speakers.

  • "lz" (log z-score) is the z-score of log f0 (Zhu 1999). Like semitones it works on ratios, so the same interval counts the same in a low and a high voice; like "zscore" it also divides by each speaker's spread, so speakers with narrow and wide pitch ranges end up on one scale. It equals semitones measured from the speaker's geometric mean (the speaker_mean that "lz" reports) divided by the speaker's SD in semitones. f0_st is measured from the arithmetic mean instead: with mean_method = "simple", f0_st / sd(f0_st) has the same shape as LZ, shifted by a small per-speaker constant; with "weighted", LZ also divides by the tone-weighted SD, so the two differ slightly in scale as well. It is the usual "z-score" in studies of tone in languages of China: 37 of the 136 studies reviewed by Xu and Zhang (2024) used it, against 4 that used a plain z-score. Because it equalises ranges, prefer semitones when differences in range are themselves of interest (e.g. comparing the size of tone spaces across speakers or varieties).

Choosing mean_method

  • "weighted" (default) lets every tone count once, regardless of how many tokens it has. The centre is the mean of the per-tone means. For the z-scores the SD is weighted the same way: each observation gets weight 1 / (number of tones x observations of its tone), as in stats::cov.wt(). This is the right default for unbalanced designs in which token counts differ across tones, common in fieldwork and naturalistic corpora. It is this package's tone-balanced variant.

  • "simple" takes the mean (and SD) of every observation for a speaker. This is the classic formula: Rose's (1987) z-score and Zhu's (1999) LZ. Choose it to reproduce published values.

The two give identical results when every tone has the same number of observations.

The SD correction

With sd_correction = TRUE (default) the z-scores use the corrected (sample) SD, dividing by n - 1 (Bessel's correction) as stats::sd() and the published formulas do; with "weighted" this is the reliability-weights correction of stats::cov.wt(method = "unbiased"), which reduces to n - 1 when every tone has the same number of observations. FALSE gives the uncorrected (population) SD, dividing by n. With "simple", or equal numbers of observations per tone, the two differ by a factor of sqrt(n / (n - 1)), negligible for a speaker with hundreds of observations. With "weighted" the factor is 1 / sqrt(1 - sum(w^2)), which is set mostly by the tone with the fewest observations: a tone with only a few frames can make it several percent. Semitones use no SD, so the argument does not affect them.

NA handling

All summary statistics use na.rm = TRUE. Sample-level NA f0 values propagate as NA in the normalised column. For "lz", f0 values of 0 or below (sometimes used to mark unvoiced frames) have no logarithm, so they are treated as NA too.

References

Rose, P. (1987). Considerations in the normalisation of the fundamental frequency of linguistic tone. Speech Communication, 6(4), 343–352. doi:10.1016/0167-6393(87)90008-1

Zhu, X. (1999). Shanghai Tonetics. LINCOM Europa.

Xu, C., & Zhang, C. (2024). A cross-linguistic review of citation tone production studies: Methodology and recommendations. The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 156(4), 2538–2565. doi:10.1121/10.0032356

See also

  • fit_polynomial(), fit_gca(), fit_gamm() for downstream contour modelling that typically operates on the normalised column.

  • contour_to_chao() for converting mean contours to Chao tone numerals, often called on normalise_f0() output.

Examples

data(sample_f0)

out <- normalise_f0(sample_f0,
                    f0      = "f0_Hz",
                    speaker = "speaker",
                    tone    = "tone",
                    method  = "semitone")
head(out[, c("speaker", "tone", "f0_Hz", "speaker_mean", "f0_st")])
#>   speaker tone    f0_Hz speaker_mean     f0_st
#> 1   dc102    3 245.7078     237.0675 0.6197450
#> 2   dc102    3 246.4516     237.0675 0.6720735
#> 3   dc102    3 247.5111     237.0675 0.7463436
#> 4   dc102    3 248.5496     237.0675 0.8188289
#> 5   dc102    3 249.7015     237.0675 0.8988754
#> 6   dc102    3 251.6647     237.0675 1.0344568

# Same data, z-score instead of semitones:
out_z <- normalise_f0(sample_f0,
                      f0      = "f0_Hz",
                      speaker = "speaker",
                      tone    = "tone",
                      method  = "zscore")
head(out_z[, c("speaker", "f0_Hz", "speaker_mean", "f0_zscore")])
#>   speaker    f0_Hz speaker_mean f0_zscore
#> 1   dc102 245.7078     237.0675 0.1935695
#> 2   dc102 246.4516     237.0675 0.2102331
#> 3   dc102 247.5111     237.0675 0.2339705
#> 4   dc102 248.5496     237.0675 0.2572359
#> 5   dc102 249.7015     237.0675 0.2830415
#> 6   dc102 251.6647     237.0675 0.3270239

# Log z-score (LZ), common in studies of Chinese tone:
out_lz <- normalise_f0(sample_f0,
                       f0      = "f0_Hz",
                       speaker = "speaker",
                       tone    = "tone",
                       method  = "lz")
head(out_lz[, c("speaker", "f0_Hz", "speaker_mean", "f0_lz")])
#>   speaker    f0_Hz speaker_mean     f0_lz
#> 1   dc102 245.7078     233.0639 0.2886142
#> 2   dc102 246.4516     233.0639 0.3051268
#> 3   dc102 247.5111     233.0639 0.3285633
#> 4   dc102 248.5496     233.0639 0.3514366
#> 5   dc102 249.7015     233.0639 0.3766959
#> 6   dc102 251.6647     233.0639 0.4194796
